OCOchem progressed the field of CO electrolysis by scaling up reactor sizes from 2 usually applied 5 to 10 cm2 to demonstrate performance to 100 cm2 and then to >300 cm2 as proposed. OCOchem completed Task 2, demonstrating the target electrochemical performance parameters (current density of 125 mA/cm2 at FE >70% for >120 hours for the 100cm2 cell). Issues with GDE flooding and catalyst activity over time have been resolved by OCO’s significant development in the areas of (a) Gen 2 carbon paper-based gas diffusion electrodes and (b) modified electrochemical reactor’s operating conditions. Thus, the go/no-go milestone for budget period 2 was met. OCOchem successfully developed, tested, and demonstrated an electrochemical cell at 540 cm2, a size exceeding the requirements of 300 cm2. The target size of the electrochemical cell was 300 cm2 (30 cm height x 10 cm width). OCOchem’s large electrochemical cell with a single panel of GDE, 36 cm height x 15 cm width (540 cm2) electrochemical (geometric) area, successfully operated with one and optimized to obtain electrochemical performance close to the target parameters. During Task 13 and Milestone 13.1, very good electrochemical performance at >300 cm2 size cell was achieved, meeting almost all the target values for all parameters for 87 hours for a 540 cm2 size GDE. The target current density of 125 mA/cm2 and voltage was higher at 4.9 V. It provided an average of 89% FE (greater than 75% target) over 87 hours, after which it dropped below 75% in discontinuous tests. Biological Upconversion Throughout the project, we achieved groundbreaking progress in developing a bioconversion process to transform C1 feedstocks into ethylene glycol. We started by identifying, characterizing, and engineering various formate activation enzymes to effectively balance the production of key intermediates, formaldehyde, and formyl-CoA, which are crucial for the subsequent condensation steps. Utilizing specially engineered 54 variants of 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA synthase (HACS), we improved the condensation process by optimizing enzyme performance at low formaldehyde concentrations, significantly enhancing the pathway's efficiency. In tandem, we integrated these pathways to optimize the synthesis of ethylene glycol directly from formate, demonstrating a robust capability to minimize by-product formation and maximize desired output. Additionally, we focused on the generation of NADH from formate to support the energy requirements of the process, ensuring a balanced redox state essential for optimal yields. The engineering of bacterial host strains also played a crucial role, as we tailored them to maximize pathway activity and minimize unwanted side reactions, including formate oxidation. This comprehensive approach led to a significant outcome: under anaerobic conditions in a bioreactor, with formate as an energy source and formaldehyde feeding, we achieved an ethylene glycol production of 2.3 g/L, more than doubling our initial target of 1 g/L. This accomplishment not only underscores the technical success of the project but also highlights its potential scalability and applicability in industrial settings, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional chemical synthesis methods.
